title: Catholic: the Mass
hookLine: Catholics believe Christ is truly present in the bread and wine
last: CHRISTMAS — A CHILD IN THE COLD.

lines: A RED CANDLE THAT NEVER GOES OUT.
cards: A Catholic church on a weekday afternoon. Quiet. A few people sit scattered in the pews, not talking, not reading, just there.

Near the front, beside a small locked box, a candle burns in red glass, day and night. Ask one of them why they came, and the answer might be a nod toward that box, and three words: because he's here.
Today, the center of it all: the Eucharist, and what Catholics call the real presence.

teach.b: Eucharist is a Greek word: thanksgiving, kin to charis, grace, from a few days ago. It names the meal at the heart of the Mass, which goes back to the night before Jesus died.
At a Passover-season supper with his disciples, he took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them.

teach.h: TAKE YE, AND EAT. THIS IS MY BODY.
teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims translation: "Take ye, and eat. This is my body." Then the cup: his blood of the covenant. And, in Luke's telling, do this in memory of me.
Catholics take those words at their plainest.
They believe that at Mass, when the priest says Jesus' words over the bread and wine, they become the body and blood of Christ: still looking and tasting like bread and wine, but truly him.
The Church's word for this, from the Middle Ages, is transubstantiation, a change in what the thing most deeply is. Hence the name: the real presence.

teach.h: THE TABERNACLE AND THE RED LAMP.
teach.b: And that's what the little box, the tabernacle, holds: consecrated bread kept after Mass, for the sick and for prayer.

teach.h: WHO SAYS WHAT ABOUT THE MEAL.
teach.b: The red lamp says someone is home. Christians understand this meal differently. Orthodox Christians also believe Christ is truly present, and prefer to call it a holy mystery rather than define how.
Lutherans speak of a real presence too, in their own terms. Many other Protestants see the meal as a powerful remembrance and sign.
The Second Vatican Council called the Eucharist the source and summit of the whole Christian life. So, for Catholics, a quiet church is never really empty.

how: Catholics are asked to attend Mass every Sunday, and some go daily, receiving Communion; many also pray quietly before the tabernacle, where a sanctuary lamp burns to show the consecrated bread is kept there.

games.q: at the last supper, Jesus takes bread and gives thanks. what does he say as he gives it?
o: take ye, and eat. this is my body.
games.why: Matthew 26:26. Catholics take the words at their plainest: this is my body.

practice: If you like, and if one is near, you can sit in a quiet church sometime this week; the doors of many are open by day.
For now, sit where you are and notice what is really here: your breath, the weight of your body, the sounds in the room. No need to add anything; just be present to what's present.
